headline: Nyatt Point after dark: bass go deep and nocturnal while scup keep the rods bent
subhead: The upper bay's running warm and quiet on top, but the ledges and the night bite are carrying the week.
body_markdown:
Ran into Dom down at the Sabin Point ramp Tuesday morning, hauling his skiff out with two schoolie bass in the cooler and that look guys get when the fishing's fine but not what it was in May. "Where's everybody at," he said, not really asking. I didn't have to tell him. The herring run through Buckeye Brook wrapped up back in April, and every bass that rode that run north through the Providence River has scattered out and gone smart on us. That's the story of the whole upper bay right now — not bad fishing, just bass that know better than to sit around in warm water during daylight.

The upper bay's been running warm on the surface for weeks now, pushing into the mid-70s off the piers and holding there under this stretch of sun and light southwest wind. That's above the comfort window for a big striper, and it's shoved the better fish off the flats and down onto structure — the Nyatt Point ledge, the drop along Conimicut Light, the deep water off Poppasquash Point, and the east side rip along Prudence Island where the bottom falls to 30, 35 feet. Those are night spots now. I've had my best luck the last two weeks on the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood, working live eels or chunked bunker on a fish-finder rig right on the bottom in that 25-to-35-foot band off Nyatt. Full dark, dead low light, that's when the bigger fish show. Daytime, you're mostly working schoolies in the 20-to-26-inch range on top of the same structure, and they'll eat a white bucktail dragged slow off the ledge, but the slot fish and up have gone strictly nocturnal. That's exactly the pattern we flagged holding steady this week, and the bay hasn't given us a reason to argue with it.

Fluke are the better daylight bet right now, and they're pushing well up into the bay chasing the same warm water that's got the bass hiding. Greenwich Bay has been quietly productive — the channel edges off Warwick Neck and the drop-off outside the cove in 18 to 25 feet are holding keeper fish mixed with a lot of shorts, which is honest summer fluke fishing, not a blitz. Same story working the Providence River shipping channel off Fields Point and down toward Conimicut Point, where the bottom drops from the flats into 25 to 30 feet of water. Drift that edge on the last of the incoming into the top of the high, dragging a chartreuse bucktail tipped with a strip of squid, or a 4-inch white Gulp on a light jighead if the current's soft. You'll pick through a bunch of small fish for every keeper, but the keepers have been decent — fish to 22, 23 inches coming out of Greenwich Bay this week.

Scup are the one thing in this bay that hasn't complicated itself at all. Rocky Point, the rock pile off Nyatt, the ledges around Prudence Island — anywhere there's structure in 15 to 25 feet, scup are stacked and eating without much fuss. Sandworms or a piece of clam belly on a high-low rig, light spinning gear, and you can fill a bucket in an hour on the right tide. This is the fishery I send beginners to right now because it's the most dependable thing going in the bay — no drama, just bent rods, best around the tide change when the current slacks enough to hold bottom without a two-ounce sinker.

Bluefish have started showing with a little more purpose the last week, working peanut bunker schools at the mouth of the Providence River and off Conimicut Point, especially in that hour around dusk when the bait balls up tight against the current line. That tracks with what's been happening the length of the coast — blues thriving in this warm water while the bass duck it — and the bay's version of it has been smaller, snapper-to-cocktail-size fish mostly, but there's been enough two-to-four-pound fish mixed in off Rocky Point to make a small metal or a Deadly Dick worth throwing if you see the surface nervous.

Weakfish and black sea bass are around but not what I'd call a target right now — a few weakfish showing up as bycatch on the fluke drifts in Greenwich Bay, and sea bass holding tight to the rockier structure off Prudence, but neither is worth a dedicated trip with everything else going on.

Looking ahead, the tide's easing off the full moon push toward neap over the next several days, which should settle the current down and make that Nyatt/Conimicut night program even more workable — softer water means you can hold bottom with less lead and fish that eel more naturally. If the sun keeps cooking the surface like it has, expect the bass to stay locked into that dawn, dusk, and full-dark pattern right through the week, with the daytime action belonging to fluke and scup. Keep an eye on the river mouth for bluefish activity building as we push toward the second week of August — if that bait keeps concentrating the way it has, the blitz windows at dusk could get a lot more interesting before the new moon on the 12th resets everything.
